messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Frank Delaney, a 71-year-old North American man, came to treatment after more than a year of trying to manage the aftermath of a terrorist attack he had witnessed while working as a security guard. The event occurred during an evening shift at a transit hub, when a blast and the panic that followed turned a routine watch into chaos: people were shouting, a woman nearby was screaming for her child, and Frank remembers ducking behind a concrete pillar while trying to account for who was injured and where the danger might come from next. What has stayed with him is not a smooth narrative but fragments that remain painfully bright and, at other moments, strangely flat. He described the memories as very clear and detailed when they come, yet he also said that sometimes he can picture the scene and feel almost nothing, as if it happened to a stranger. He could not tell a clear story of the event even to himself, only pieces that return in no reliable order.

In the weeks after the attack, Frank began to judge himself harshly for how he had handled it. He became convinced that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation, that he had failed in his most important role in life, and that he could not deal with even the slightest upset. Those conclusions shaped what he did next: he started choosing seats with his back to the wall so he could see the whole room, scanning for exits and for anyone who looked dangerous. At work, he would stand where he could watch people enter the building, and in restaurants or church basements he was quick to claim a corner seat before anyone else could. He told himself that if he stayed alert enough, he might prevent another disaster, but the vigilance also kept him trapped in the belief that he was weak and inadequate, always one step behind what a capable man should have managed.

That way of living began to narrow his world. Frank found himself ruminating for hours about how to get even with the assailant, imagining retaliation with a grim, restless focus that he knew would never be carried out. The more he sat with those thoughts, the more they seemed to confirm his own judgment that he was not coping, that a man in his position should be steadier, tougher, more in control. He would replay the night of the attack in his mind, but because he was always scanning the room or rehearsing revenge, the memory never settled into a coherent account. Instead, it remained a series of vivid images and numb blanks, made harder to organize by the constant effort to stay on guard. Sitting with his back to the wall became less a preference than a rule, a habit that followed him into the diner where he met his wife for breakfast, the waiting room at the clinic, and the side chair in the chapel before Sunday service.

Over time, these patterns took a toll on his marriage and his work. His wife noticed that he was hard to reach, preoccupied, and less willing to go out unless he could control where he sat. At work, he became more distant with coworkers and less confident in routine assignments, convinced that a single unexpected disturbance would expose his limits. He was especially distressed by the fact that the very measures he used to feel safer seemed to keep proving his fears: the more he watched for danger, the more dangerous the world felt, and the more dangerous it felt, the more he judged himself as someone who could not manage it. Even his memories seemed to follow that pattern, arriving as sharp, detailed flashes or as numb, disconnected pieces, never as a story he could hold together and put in the past.

Frank finally sought help after realizing he was spending nearly every day arranging his life around the attack. He said he was tired of measuring every room, every face, and every movement against the possibility of another assault, and tired of feeling that he had failed as a protector in the one role that had given his life structure. What he fears most is that he will never feel steady again, and what he hopes for is a way to remember what happened without being pulled back into it every time he walks into a room.
